subject: BRGSA
subjectTitle: Business Research and Growth Systems Architecture

sections.rule: One correct option. Two marks each. No negative marking.
A short scenario, then a task. Both parts must be right for the marks. No partial credit.
A complete structured response. Not machine-marked.

paper.caselet: A B2B tool loses 4% of accounts a month. Exit interviews with 30 leavers find 19 never completed the initial data import, 7 left when their internal champion changed job, and 4 said a competitor was cheaper. The team is preparing a discount offer for accounts showing low usage.
paper.stem: What should the team do instead?
options: Proceed with the discount, because price is the only cause a company can act on directly and quickly
Fix the import and build a second contact inside each account, since price explains four of thirty departures
Survey the remaining accounts before acting, since thirty interviews is too small a base for any decision
Accept 4% as the market rate for this category and concentrate the effort on winning replacement accounts

paper.caselet: A subscription product reports that overall month-3 retention has held at 38% for a year, and the team is treating the product as stable. Split by signup month, the January cohort retained 47% at month three, April 39%, July 33% and October 28%. Monthly signups have roughly tripled over the same year.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The October cohort is simply too young to judge, so the fall is an artefact of measuring groups at different ages
Signups tripling is the finding, and the retention split is a consequence of serving a larger and more varied market than before
Each new cohort is retaining worse than the one before it, and rising signup volume is holding the blended figure flat
Retention is stable, since the aggregate figure has not moved across a full year of trading and that is the measure of the product

paper.caselet: A D2C brand validates demand with paid pre-orders. Its first cohort activates through a 21-day routine, repurchase predicts retention, and acquisition is profitable. The team now has ten experiment ideas but capacity for two.
paper.stem: Which sequence best protects the evidence chain?
options: Choose the two ideas with the highest reach scores and run them
Run all ten with smaller samples each
Optimise for the total follower count across all channels instead
Name the current constraint, score ideas against it with evidence/capacity, pre-register decisions, then reallocate after results

paper.caselet: Two landing pages report the same 8% signup rate. Page A was shown to the stated ICP through targeted traffic. Page B was sent to friends, employees, and a prize-seeking giveaway list.
paper.stem: Which conclusion is defensible?
options: Both pages prove exactly equal demand because the measured conversion rate is identical
Page B carries the stronger signal because its audience was larger
Page A carries the more trustworthy demand signal because the traffic matches the intended market
Neither page can ever be used for validation because landing pages are not real products

paper.stem: Which order best represents the course's defensible growth chain?
options: Scale spend → validate demand → retain users → choose a metric → monetize → operate the whole system
Validate demand → run trustworthy experiments → read cohorts/economics → fix constraint → activate/retain → monetize → operate
Acquire users → count signups → add pricing tiers → survey customers → scale the spend
Build the product fully → choose a channel → define the customer → then measure the results at the end

paper.caselet: A complex enterprise product needs security review, multi-stakeholder approval, custom integration, and a high annual contract.
paper.stem: Which primary motion is better matched?
options: Pure self-serve PLG with no human support
Consumer referral coupons on their own, with no sales involvement at any deal size
No deliberate acquisition motion of any kind
Sales-led growth supported by product experience

paper.stem: What makes lean validation different from simply doing more market research?
options: It replaces customer evidence with the founder's own judgment about the problem
It estimates the total addressable market from desk research before speaking to any real buyers
It always turns the demand assumption into a test whose threshold is set before any build
It begins only after the product is complete and ready to put in front of customers

paper.stem: Why must a B2B pipeline define entry and exit criteria for each stage?
options: To increase the number of email opens recorded across each outreach sequence sent to the list
So conversion always reflects real buyer progress and never a subjective sales label
To make the CRM records look complete and tidy for internal reporting purposes each quarter
To avoid having to speak to customers directly at any point in the process

paper.stem: When does a list of experiment ideas become an operating backlog?
options: When it has grown to more than a hundred rows in the sheet
When the ideas have all been sorted neatly into alphabetical order
When each item carries the fields needed to prioritize, run, own, and decide it
When nobody is allowed to remove an idea

paper.stem: An early startup has no repeatable channel and uncertain retention. Which move fits its stage?
options: Maximise automation everywhere before making direct customer contact
Optimise quarterly media efficiency at scale across paid channels
Build a large specialist growth organisation immediately
Run founder-close, high-learning tests to find repeatability

paper.caselet: Traffic is healthy, signup conversion is healthy, but only 12% of new accounts complete the first value event. The team proposes buying more ads.
paper.stem: What should the growth diagnosis prioritize?
options: More top-of-funnel traffic volume
A lower sample-size target
Activation—the narrowest current constraint
A full company rebrand exercise

paper.stem: A useful pricing change genuinely improves conversion, but an underpowered test concludes that nothing changed. Which error is this?
options: A Type I error, a false positive
No error because the result was not significant
Survivorship bias alone, with no testing error involved
A Type II error, a false negative

paper.caselet: A SaaS company grows 35% through new sales, but the starting cohort falls from ₹20 lakh to ₹16 lakh MRR after expansion, churn, and downgrades.
paper.stem: What does the cohort's NRR say?
options: NRR is 125%, so the revenue base is compounding
NRR cannot be calculated without new sales figures
NRR is 80%; acquisition is masking a shrinking base
NRR is 35% for this cohort

paper.stem: For a team-based B2B SaaS product, which retention unit is usually more decision-useful than counting individual logins alone?
options: The count of social media followers
The total number of website visitors
Every employee working in the addressable market
The paying account or team

paper.stem: Which evidence should receive the greatest weight in a build/no-build decision?
options: Strong founder confidence in the idea's eventual commercial success in the market
A large total number of advertising impressions delivered to the market so far
High levels of enthusiasm expressed in a survey
Commitments from target customers under an offer with real terms

paper.stem: Which response is the strongest evidence that a customer is likely to buy?
options: Opening the product email
A like on the announcement
‘A great idea’ in a survey
A refundable pre-order placed under clear terms

paper.stem: Which statement correctly separates referral from a network effect?
options: They are exactly the same thing whenever users invite their friends to join the product themselves
Referral always improves the product's value for the users who already have it installed on their devices
Referral acquires another user; a network effect makes the product more valuable as relevant users join
Network effects always require some form of paid incentive before they will begin to work properly at all

paper.stem: What is the purpose of a 70/20/10 portfolio split across known winners, new bets, and exploratory options?
options: To balance exploitation with learning under constrained capacity
To guarantee that every experiment run will succeed
To spend seventy percent of the budget on the newest idea
To prevent any reallocation of budget mid-quarter

paper.caselet: A team spends ₹2,00,000 on a paid channel. Their average contract value is ₹1,000 a month and their acquisition cost on that channel lands near ₹8,000.
paper.stem: What should the team do?
options: Improve the creative and the targeting first, since a high acquisition cost usually reflects a weak campaign rather than the channel.
Keep the channel and raise the price, since a contract worth more would make the same acquisition cost acceptable.
Stop the channel on price-point mismatch, because that arithmetic is settled before any creative decision is taken.
Continue for a full quarter, because paid channels need time before their true cost per customer can be judged.

paper.caselet: An experiment hypothesised activation moving from 34% to 45%. It lands at 38%, and the team wants to keep iterating.
paper.stem: What settles whether to continue?
options: Whether another variation could plausibly close the remaining gap, which is the test for a worthwhile iteration.
Whether the team has capacity, since a live experiment that is improving the number is worth keeping while resources allow.
The thresholds written before the experiment went live, since all four parts of the rule are agreed in advance.
Whether 38% is a statistically significant improvement over 34%, which is what decides if the effect is real.

paper.caselet: An onboarding A/B test is planned for 1,400 users per variant at alpha 0.05, but the preferred version leads after eighteen visitors in each group.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Run both variants to the pre-calculated sample and apply the declared threshold before deciding, however persuasive the interim dashboard looks. (A/B testing and statistical significance)
Increase alpha after seeing the lead, so the same data can cross a threshold that better reflects the team's confidence in the new design. (A/B testing and statistical significance)
Replace the planned sample with the total number of signups across both variants, because the experiment has already collected enough users overall. (A/B testing and statistical significance)
Stop the A/B test and ship the leader, because an early advantage is direct evidence and waiting only delays the value already visible in the dashboard. (A/B testing and statistical significance)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: A/B testing and statistical significance: A/B testing earns statistical significance only after the planned sample is reached, using the baseline, minimum detectable effect and alpha fixed before either variant's result is visible.

A/B testing and statistical significance: Test modes follow the stakes: an expensive wrong decision needs a valid test run to its sample, while a low-stakes choice may use a directional test that is reported as suggestive rather than conclusive.

A/B testing and statistical significance: A Type I error scales something that does not work; a Type II error abandons something that does. Every test outcome lands in one of the four cells of that matrix.

A/B testing and statistical significance: An experiment starts from the null position that nothing changed, and the variant earns the decision only when evidence collected to a pre-set sample is strong enough to reject it.

paper.caselet: A meeting assistant promises that follow-ups are ready before a meeting ends, yet most new users never record a meeting and the team optimises profile completion instead.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Call signup the AHA and optimise acquisition, since every later value event depends on the user entering the product first. (AHA moment and time to AHA)

Use profile completion as the AHA because more retained users complete profiles, without testing whether pushing profile completion changes retention or delivers the promised outcome. (AHA moment and time to AHA)

Define the first recorded meeting as the AHA candidate, test whether moving users toward it improves retention, and shorten the path to that event rather than to profile completion. (AHA moment and time to AHA)
Add more onboarding steps explaining every feature, because a longer tour makes users more informed before they reach the promised value. (AHA moment and time to AHA)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: AHA moment and time to AHA: Activation is the first observable moment a user experiences the promised value, and every step standing between signup and that moment sheds a share of the users still remaining.

AHA moment and time to AHA: The AHA moment is the first countable event where the product's promised value actually happens, and time to AHA is the elapsed path from first use to that event that onboarding should compress.

AHA moment and time to AHA: Lean validation asks whether real people will take a real action on a real offer before the product is built; the build trap spends the full cost to learn the same thing afterwards.

AHA moment and time to AHA: Every channel has fixed properties — targeting, control, input cost, output quality, time to result and economics — and it fits only when those match the product's buyer and unit economics.

paper.caselet: An experiment will reach its sample in week five, but the roadmap lists only active experiments and leaves the decision date, dependency and slack unrecorded.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Allocate the slack to another experiment immediately, so every week looks fully utilised before any dependency or overrun is known. (90-day growth roadmap)
Treat the ranked backlog as the calendar and start whichever experiment has the highest ICE score whenever capacity appears. (90-day growth roadmap)
Add the week-five decision date now, show the dependency and capacity committed, and preserve visible slack so an overrun does not silently consume the next experiment. (90-day growth roadmap)
Wait until week five to schedule the decision, because committing now would force the team to act before it knows how clear the result will be. (90-day growth roadmap)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: 90-day growth roadmap: A 90-day growth roadmap turns the experiment backlog into twelve weeks of active work, capacity, decision dates and dependencies, with each date committed before the quarter begins.

90-day growth roadmap: The growth operating system joins ICE, backlog, decision rules, real metrics, resource allocation and the roadmap across AARRR, and its master loop makes the output of one stage the input of the next cycle.
90-day growth roadmap: The golden rule is to decide before the experiment runs: a metric earns its place only with an owner, a threshold and the action already agreed for crossing it.

90-day growth roadmap: ICE scores each idea on impact against the current constraint, confidence backed by evidence that can be named, and ease including the time to a credible signal, turning a list of ideas into an ordered backlog.

paper.caselet: A funded SaaS company has an eighteen-month payback period and proposes doubling acquisition because its LTV:CAC ratio is healthy.
paper.stem: Fill both parts of the recommendation so the action and framework agree.

blanks.label: Choose the decision
options: Double acquisition now, because eventual lifetime value proves every new customer is profitable and the timing of the cash return cannot change the growth decision. (Payback scaling threshold)
Use revenue rather than gross profit in payback, which will shorten the period without changing acquisition cost, pricing or the cost of serving the customer. (Payback scaling threshold)
Improve CAC, ARPU or gross margin until payback fits the company's capital and motion before scaling the acquisition budget. (Payback scaling threshold)
Treat eighteen months as safe for every company, because the twelve-month mark is only a reporting convention and has no link to cash recycling. (Payback scaling threshold)

blanks.label: Choose the framework
options: Payback scaling threshold: Revenue crosses several team handoffs, and each needs an entry criterion, an owner, the context that must travel with it and a response-time SLA; payback measures how long acquisition cash stays tied up before gross profit returns it.

Payback scaling threshold: Revenue architecture chooses product-led growth for high-volume, lower-value transactions and sales-led growth for lower-volume, higher-value deals, with the cycle and team matched to the motion.

Payback scaling threshold: The scaling threshold is a payback period below twelve months for a typical funded company: acquisition cash returns as gross profit within a year and can be recycled before growth consumes more capital than it returns.

Payback scaling threshold: Pricing is a structure rather than a number: tiers, units, limits and packaging decide how customers enter, upgrade and expand, and NRR measures whether the existing base grows without counting new customers.

paper.caselet: A fleet-tracking company has capacity for six engineering projects this quarter and forty candidate ideas. The chief executive is pressing for a public API, which is highly visible, carries an eight-week estimate, has been requested by two prospects and no existing customer, and has no identified effect on any current metric. A second candidate, a two-week change collapsing a six-step vehicle-onboarding flow to two steps, is supported by session recordings of nineteen customers abandoning at step four; the company's own data shows fleets that finish onboarding within seven days renew at three times the rate of those that do not, and 41% currently finish inside seven days. A third would rebuild the marketing-to-sales handoff, where 210 qualified leads produced 96 accepted, the definition of the remaining 114 has never been agreed between the two teams, and first contact averages six days. Nobody at the company has spoken to a churned customer in eleven months; the head of product declined a proposed round of interviews as anecdotal. Ideas are currently ranked in a spreadsheet by a single enthusiasm score contributed by whoever proposed them.
paper.stem: Write the recommendation for how this quarter's six slots should be decided, and what should be in them. Deal with the chief executive's proposal explicitly.

paper.caselet: A direct-to-consumer coffee brand sells a ₹1,150 monthly subscription. To arrest a decline it ran a 30% launch discount for first-time subscribers. Signups rose 240% during the eight-week offer and the growth lead has proposed making the discount permanent, citing contribution margin that stayed positive throughout. The cohort numbers were not in that proposal. Discounted subscribers cancel at 58% by month three against 21% for full-price subscribers, and 4% ever accept the price increase at renewal. Blended acquisition cost is ₹1,900. Full-price subscribers contribute about ₹430 a month against ₹180 for discounted ones. Separately the team has a backlog of eleven ideas and capacity for three: the permanent discount, a ₹1,900 twin-bag tier that 340 customers have asked for by email, and a packaging redesign the founder favours which no customer has mentioned and which would take nine weeks. There is no tier above the single plan today.
paper.stem: Write the recommendation on the discount and on which three ideas should be built. Say plainly what the signup figure did and did not demonstrate.
